title: Aisha's necklace
hookLine: a lost necklace, a vicious rumor, and verses clearing Aisha (24:11–20)

lines: A NECKLACE, LOST IN THE DARK.
cards: A rumor starts as one sentence from one person. Then it's in three group chats. By evening, people who've never met the person involved are sure what happened, and nobody can say who said it first.
In Medina, a rumor like that fastened onto Aisha, the wife of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. She told the story herself, in a long account kept in Sahih al-Bukhari. It started with something tiny.
On the way home from a journey, in the dark, she realized her necklace was gone.

teach.b: Aisha went back to look for it. While she was gone, the men who carried her curtained litter lifted it onto the camel, thinking she was inside. She was young and light, she said, and they didn't notice.
The army left. She came back to an empty camp, sat down, and fell asleep.
A companion named Safwan, riding behind the army, found her in the morning, let her ride his camel, and walked it by the reins until they caught up. That was all.
But some people in Medina saw them arrive together, and a few began to talk. The story grew. Aisha got sick and didn't know what was being said about her for weeks.
When she found out, she cried for two nights without sleeping.
The Prophet waited, and no revelation came for a month.
Finally she said she could only say what Jacob said when his sons came with their lie about Joseph: patience is beautiful, and God is the one to ask for help. Then the verses came, in Surah an-Nur.
They cleared her, and they turned on the rumor itself. Why, when you heard it, didn't you think well of your own people and say, this is an obvious lie?
You passed it from tongue to tongue, and took it lightly, and to God it was enormous. Sunni Muslims read these verses as clearing Aisha.
Some Shia commentators connect them to a different accusation, against another of the Prophet's household.
Both read in them the same command: don't carry it.

how: Muslim teachers use the story of the ifk, the slander, and 24:11–20 as the Qur'an's core teaching against spreading unverified accusations and gossip.

o: a small loss that set off a cruel rumor about Aisha
a family heirloom Aisha gave away to the poor
a wedding gift the Prophet gave Aisha in Medina

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: walked the camel by the reins

s: the verses came the next day
about a month passed with no revelation.
it's her own account, kept in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim.
they also turn on the rumor: why didn't you think well of your own and call it a lie?

games.q: you've heard the rumor about Aisha in Medina. everyone's talking. what do the verses say you should have done?
o: ask around to find out more.
think well of her and say, this is an obvious lie.
games.why: the verses ask why, when they heard it, believers didn't think well of their own and say, this is a plain lie.

practice: Think of something you've heard about someone lately that you don't actually know is true, and notice the little itch to tell it.
Picture it stopping with you, and the words you'd say instead, close to the verse's own: it's not for us to speak of this. If you pray, you can ask God to guard your tongue.

wordCard.voice: Aisha's necklace. The small loss that set off a cruel rumor, and the verses in Surah an-Nur that answered it. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the slander, the lie. the name Muslims give this whole episode.

carryVoice: Your line: don't carry the rumor. A story can stop with you. Day two hundred sixty-nine, done.
